segments.t: In the conference room of ASK, movie star Jean Reno brings champagne to express his gratitude to the agency staff. Meeting him alone, Andrea Martel confides that she is resigning from agent life to start a new chapter. Let's listen to their conversation in French first.
C'est pour vous remercier tous!
Merci Jean, c'est très gentil.
J'ai quelque chose à te dire.
Tu as l'air grave, Andréa.
Je pars de l'agence.
Tu quittes ce métier?
Oui, je m'en vais définitivement.
C'est une vie de chien.
Mais toi, tu dois continuer.
Seulement si le film se fait!
Élise Formain est une femme redoutable.
Ne t'inquiète pas pour moi.
Prends bien soin de ton talent.
Bonne chance pour ta nouvelle vie!
Let's examine the conversation line by line and explore the French expressions.
C'est pour vous remercier tous!
'It is to thank you all!' Jean Reno presents champagne and treats to the team. Dropping the subject pronoun turns the verb for 'to thank' into a direct, punchy command.
Merci Jean, c'est très gentil.
'Thank you Jean, that is very kind.' Andrea appreciates the generous thought. In spoken French, the little word before 'the next word' drops its final vowel and attaches with an apostrophe.
J'ai quelque chose à te dire.
'I have something to tell you.' Andrea shifts the mood with a serious announcement. This conversational past tense combines a helper verb with the past participle for 'to have'.
Tu as l'air grave, Andréa.
'You look serious, Andrea.' Jean notices her solemn expression. Notice how 'to have' leads directly into the noun meaning 'air'.
Je pars de l'agence.
'I am leaving the agency.' The verb meaning 'to leave' pairs naturally with the noun for 'agency' in everyday conversation.
Tu quittes ce métier?
'Are you quitting this job?' Jean asks in genuine astonishment. The informal 'you' form around 'to leave' marks a direct, personal relationship.
Oui, je m'en vais définitivement.
'Yes, I am leaving definitively.' Andrea confirms that her agent career is over. Notice how the short vowel drops before a vowel sound around 'to go', making the phrase flow smoothly as one unit.
C'est une vie de chien.
'It is a dog's life.' Jean remarks on the exhausting demands of talent representation. The key noun here means 'life', anchored by its matching French article.
Mais toi, tu dois continuer.
'But you, you must go on.' Andrea urges him to stay dedicated to cinema. Andrea uses the casual singular 'you' with 'must', showing close familiarity.
Seulement si le film se fait!
'Only if the movie happens!' Jean conditions his continuation on good cinema. Dropping the subject pronoun turns the verb for 'to do' into a direct, punchy command.
Élise Formain est une femme redoutable.
'Elise Formain is a formidable woman.' Andrea warns him about rival management. Notice how 'to be' leads directly into the noun meaning 'woman'.
Ne t'inquiète pas pour moi.
'Do not worry about me.' Jean reassures her with his veteran wisdom. Notice the classic French sandwich negation wrapping right around 'to worry'.
Prends bien soin de ton talent.
'Take good care of your talent.' Andrea gives her final parting wish as an agent. The verb meaning 'to take' pairs naturally with the noun for 'care' in everyday conversation.
Bonne chance pour ta nouvelle vie!

'Good luck for your new life!' Jean raises a glass to her brave next chapter. The informal 'you' form around 'luck' marks a direct, personal relationship. Now let's listen to the complete discussion once more to reinforce the vocabulary.

As Jean Reno and Andrea clink glasses in the agency boardroom, an era quietly draws to a close. When you watch the episode, listen out for the expressions meaning 'to thank' and 'kind'. You'll catch them now. See you next time.
Merci pour tout ce que tu as fait!
